text: The bell for lunch break rings at Meridian Public School, and within a minute the corridor smells of six different homes. Aarav opens his tiffin — lemon rice, still warm. Ira opens hers — two rotis and a bowl of dal. From the next bench comes the smell of fish curry, from the bench behind, of dhokla.
Aarav looks around the room and thinks: everyone here is eating something different. Everyone here is hungry at the same time, and everyone will feel better in ten minutes.
So what is actually happening inside all those tiffin boxes? Why does food make us able to run, and think, and grow?
Look at your own lunch today. Name three things in it. Where did each one come from?
3.1 What Do We Eat in a Week?
Aarav's question is a good one, and the honest answer is that we cannot say much about food in general until we look at food in particular. So begin with the food you know best: your own.

Most of us eat without paying attention. We eat what is served, at the time it is served, and we rarely notice the pattern. But there is pattern. Over a week, your meals repeat, vary, and cluster in ways that tell you something about your household, your region, and your health.

Scientists call this kind of careful watching observation. Observation is not the same as looking. Looking is what you do all day. Observing is looking with a question in mind, and writing down what you find.

title: Activity 3.1 — Keep a food diary
items: You will need: your notebook, seven days.
1. Create a food diary in your notebook, with one entry for each day.
2. Every evening for one week, write down everything you ate that day — meals, snacks, drinks, everything. Do not leave out the biscuit you ate at 4 p.m.
3. Write it the same evening. If you wait till Sunday and try to remember Monday, your data will be wrong, and wrong data is worse than no data.
4. At the end of the week, read the whole table at once.

text: In your notebook, use two columns: Day and What I ate and drank. Record one entry for each day, Monday to Sunday.
caption: Table 3.1 — My food diary

text: Now read your table as a scientist would. Did the same items appear on most days? Which days were different from the rest, and can you say why — a festival, a guest, a day you were unwell?

Next, compare. Ask three classmates to show you their tables. Find one food that appears in all four diaries, and one food that appears in only one. Comparing is how we tell what is common from what is particular.

You will almost certainly find both. Some foods — rice or wheat, dal, milk, oil, salt, sugar — turn up in nearly every diary in the class. Others turn up in one diary only, because one family cooks that dish and the others do not.
So even inside a single classroom, food is not one thing. It varies. The next question is why.
3.1.1 Food varies from place to place

If a single classroom holds this much variety, country of this size holds far more. A traveller who ate breakfast in Amritsar, lunch in Bengaluru and dinner in Imphal would eat three meals with almost nothing in common.
That is not an accident, and it is not only a matter of taste. Let us gather the evidence first and explain it afterwards.

title: Activity 3.2 — Map the food of India
items: 1. Choose four states of India. Include your own.
2. For each one, find out: which crops are grown there, which dishes are traditionally eaten, and what people commonly drink.
3. Use your library, the internet, and — best of all — people. Ask a classmate whose family comes from another state. Ask a neighbour.
4. Record your findings in your notebook using the headings in Table 3.2. The printed rows are examples.

Ragi, rice, jowar, coconut, coffee, pulses
Ragi mudde, sambar, bisi bele bath, dosa, idli
Filter coffee, buttermilk, tender coconut water
Masor tenga, khar, fish curry, pitha, rice

caption: Table 3.2 — Crops and food across Indian states

text: Now analyse your completed table. Read down the "crops" column and then down the "dishes" column, and look for a relationship between the two.

The relationship is hard to miss. Punjab grows wheat, and Punjabi food is built on wheat. Karnataka grows ragi, and ragi appears in Karnataka's everyday meals. Manipur grows rice and bamboo, and both turn up on the Manipuri plate.

This makes sense once you think about where food has to travel from. For most of human history, and for most families even today, the cheapest and freshest food is the food grown nearby. A cuisine is, in large part, a set of clever answers to the question: what can we cook with what grows here?

And what grows here depends on two things a farmer cannot choose — the soil and the climate. Rice needs standing water and warmth. Ragi tolerates poor soil and low rainfall. Mustard grows in cool northern winters. India has an unusual range of soils and climates, which is exactly why it has an unusual range of food.

Soil and climate are not the whole story. Culture, religion and history all shape what a community eats and what it avoids. Two families in the same street, growing food from the same fields, may cook very differently.
so regional food is explained by cultivation, and then modified by taste, culture and tradition.
Name one dish that is eaten in your state but not in the state next to it. What grows in your state that might explain it?
3.1.2 Food also varies from time to time

Food varies across the map. Does it also vary across the years? Ask the oldest person you can reach, and you will find that it does — not just the dishes, but the whole business of cooking. The tools have changed, the fuel has changed, the time it takes has changed.

title: Activity 3.3 — Interview an elder
items: 1. Choose someone at least fifty years older than you — a grandparent, a neighbour, a retired teacher.

2. Prepare your questions before you meet them. Write them down. Good starting points: What did you eat as a child that you still eat today? What did you eat then that you never eat now? How was the food cooked, and on what? How long did the cooking take? What changed, and when did it change?
3. Listen more than you talk. Write their answers in their words, not yours.
4. Bring your notes to class and pool them with your classmates'.

text: Cooking tools, then and now

caption: Fig. 3.1 · (a) Chulha — traditional wood-fired stove (b) Modern gas stove

text: Pool the class's interview notes and a shared picture appears. The way food is prepared — what we can call culinary practice — has changed sharply within living memory.

Fifty years ago most Indian households cooked over a chulha burning wood, dung cakes or coal (Fig. 3.1 a). Someone had to gather the fuel, light the fire, and tend it. Today most households cook on a gas stove that lights in one second and goes out in one second (Fig. 3.1b). Spices and grain were once ground by hand on a sil-batta, a heavy stone slab worked with a stone roller (Fig. 3.1 c). Now a mixer-grinder does the same work in a minute (Fig. 3.1d).
Why did all this change?
Partly because the technology arrived. Gas connections, electricity and affordable appliances reached ordinary households, and once a tool that saves an hour a day is available, people use it.

Partly because transport improved. Roads, railways and cold storage mean that a fruit grown in Himachal can be sold in Chennai. Foods that were once purely local became available everywhere, and cuisines began to borrow from each other.
And partly because communication changed. Recipes now travel by television, phone and internet. A dish that belonged to one region for three hundred years can spread across the country in a season.

Change of this kind brings real gains. Cooking takes less time — which matters most to the women who have historically done most of it. Fuel-efficient stoves mean less smoke indoors, and less smoke means healthier lungs.

It also brings losses. Some traditional grains and dishes are disappearing, and with them the knowledge of how to cook them. Some of those grains, as we will see later in this chapter, were more nourishing than what replaced them.

Smoke in the kitchen A wood or dung chulha burning indoors fills a kitchen with fine smoke. Breathing that smoke for years damages the lungs and the heart, and the person standing closest to the stove breathes the most of it. This is one reason governments have worked to bring clean cooking fuel to rural households: a better stove is a health measure, not just a convenience.
3.2 What Is Food Made Of?

Aarav skips breakfast on Wednesday. By the second period he cannot follow what the teacher is saying, and by the third his hands feel unsteady. At break, Ira gives him half a banana. Within a few minutes he feels roughly human again.
Half a banana. A few minutes. Something in that banana reached his blood fast enough to change how he felt in class.

Something in food, then, is not the same as food. When we eat a banana we are not eating "banana" as far as the body is concerned. We are eating a mixture of substances, each of which the body uses for a different job. These substances are the components of food.
Different foods carry different components in different amounts. That is why no single food keeps a person well, and why the mixture on the plate matters as much as the items on it.
Start with the component that rescued Aarav.
Carbohydrates

Glucose is the simplest sugar the body runs on, and it is a carbohydrate. Carbohydrates are the body's main source of quick energy. This is why a marathon runner drinks glucose water during a race rather than eating a meal: glucose needs almost no processing before the muscles can use it.

We rarely eat pure glucose. We eat carbohydrates in the form of cereals — wheat, rice, maize, jowar; in root vegetables — potato and sweet potato; and in fruits — banana, mango, pineapple, sugarcane. Ordinary table sugar is a carbohydrate too.
Fats

In winter, many Indian households make laddoos. The reason is not only that they taste good. A laddoo is built from flour, ghee, goond, nuts and seeds. Ghee is a fat, and so are the cooking oils in every Indian kitchen — groundnut, mustard, coconut, sunflower, soya bean, sesame. Fats do the same essential job as carbohydrates — they supply energy — but they do it differently. Gram for gram, fat carries more than twice the energy of carbohydrate, and the body stores it rather than burning it at once. Fat is stored energy: the reserve the body draws on when food is not coming in, and part of how it keeps warm. That is why a laddoo belongs to winter. It is dense, slow energy at the time of year the body needs most of it.

Fats come from plants and from animals. Plant sources include groundnut, walnut, cashew, almond, pistachio, coconut, sesame seed, pumpkin seed, sunflower seed, soya bean and the oils pressed from them. Animal sources include butter, ghee, curd and milk.

The bear that does not eat for months Before winter, a polar bear eats heavily and builds a thick layer of fat under its skin. Through the long winter it may eat almost nothing, living off that stored fat while the same layer keeps it warm. Stored fat is a survival strategy, not a flaw — which is worth remembering before deciding that all fat is bad.
Name three foods you ate this week that contained a visible fat. Where did each fat come from — a plant or an animal?
Proteins
Carbohydrates and fats keep a body running. Neither one builds it.

Consider what a body has to do besides move. A six-year-old grows into a sixteen-year-old. A cut on your hand closes over in a week. Hair grows, nails grow, muscle thickens with training. All of that is construction work, and construction needs material.
The material is protein.

Proteins are used to build new tissue and repair damaged tissue. This is why the diet of a growing child must contain enough protein, and why an athlete training for strength needs more than a person who is not. A body short of protein cannot grow properly, however much energy it is given — you cannot build a wall out of firewood.

Plant sources of protein include all pulses — moong, tuar dal, gram, kidney beans, peas — along with soya bean, groundnut and other nuts and seeds. Animal sources include milk, curd, paneer, cheese, egg, fish, chicken and meat. Edible mushrooms are a good source too.
Because of the job they do, protein-rich foods are called body-building foods — while carbohydrates and fats, which supply energy, are together called energy-giving foods.

caption: Fig. 3.4 · Plant sources (left) and animal sources (right)

text: Which foods in your Table 3.1 diary were body-building foods? Did every day of the week contain at least one?

Mushrooms Mushrooms are not plants. They belong to a separate group of living things — fungi — and they grow in dark, damp places without sunlight. Edible mushrooms are a good source of protein, which is unusual for a food that is neither a pulse nor an animal product.
3.3 The Components We Need in Tiny Amounts

Carbohydrates, fats and proteins are the components we eat by the spoonful. There is another set that we need in amounts so small they are measured in milligrams — and yet a person who goes without them falls seriously ill.
The strongest way to see what these components do is to look at what happens when they are missing. Read the two cases below and work out the answer yourself before reading on.
Case 1 — The sailors' disease

On long sea voyages in earlier centuries, sailors fell ill in a particular way. Their gums swelled and bled, their teeth loosened, old wounds reopened, and many died — often months from any battle or storm.
In 1746, during a voyage, the Scottish physician James Lind made a careful observation. Sailors who were given lemons and oranges recovered. Sailors who were not, did not.
The condition is called scurvy.

Now interpret Case 1. Lind's sailors were not short of food — ships carried salted meat and dry biscuit in quantity. They were short of something present in lemons and oranges and absent from salted meat.

That something is now called Vitamin C. Scurvy is caused by a lack of Vitamin C in the diet, and it is prevented and cured by foods that contain it — citrus fruits like lemon and orange, and also amla, guava and green chilli.

Notice how much Lind's method matters. He did not guess. He compared two groups of sailors who differed in one respect, and drew a conclusion from the difference. That is an experiment, conducted at sea in 1746, and it saved a great many lives.
Lind's sailors ate plenty of food and still fell ill. What does that tell you about the difference between eating enough and eating well?
Case 2 — The swelling in the neck

In the 1960s, Indian scientists studying the Himalayan region and the northern plains found that a large number of people there had a visible swelling at the front of the neck. It was common in some districts and rare in others only a few hundred kilometres away.
Following the scientists' findings, the Government of India promoted the addition of iodine to common salt — iodised salt. Where people switched to it, the swellings became far less common.
The condition is called goitre.

Infer what was happening. The affected regions were not short of food. What they were short of was iodine — and the shortage began in the soil. Where soil is low in iodine, the crops grown in it are low in iodine, and the water is too. People eating a local diet in such a region simply cannot get enough, no matter how much they eat.

Iodised salt solves this neatly. Salt is one of the few things that almost every household buys and almost every person eats daily, whatever else is on the plate. Adding a trace of iodine to salt reaches nearly everyone.
You have probably read the words "iodised salt" on a packet without thinking about them. They mean common salt to which a small measured quantity of iodine salts has been added.
Vitamin C and iodine are examples of a larger group: the vitamins and minerals.

The people who farm salt In the Little Rann of Kutch in Gujarat, a community called the Agariyas has produced salt for generations. For about eight months each year they live out on the salt flats in extreme desert heat, channelling seawater into shallow pans and working the crystallised salt by hand. The salt in your kitchen has a maker, and the work is punishing.

Vitamin C and iodine are two of many. Each vitamin and each mineral has its own job, its own food sources, and its own set of symptoms when the body runs short. Together they are what keep the body's defences and daily processes working.
Fig. 3.5 sets out the main ones. Read it carefully — you will be using it again in the exercises at the end of the chapter.

title: Activity 3.4 — A survey in your neighbourhood
items: Carry out this activity under your teacher's guidance.
1. Study Fig. 3.5 until you know the symptoms listed for each nutrient.

2. Talk to people in your neighbourhood — with their permission, and politely. Ask whether they have noticed any of these symptoms in themselves or their family: trouble seeing in dim light, bleeding gums, weakness and breathlessness, aching or bending bones.
3. Where someone reports a symptom, ask — again, politely — what they usually eat. Look for a food group that is largely missing.
4. Correlate the two. Which deficiency would fit the symptoms and the diet together?
5. Suggest which foods, easily available and affordable locally, could help.
6. Always end by suggesting they see a doctor.

A warning that matters. You are not diagnosing anyone. A symptom can have many causes, and only a doctor can test and treat. Your job here is to practise linking evidence to explanation — and then to hand the matter to someone qualified.

text: Look back over everything named so far: carbohydrates, fats, proteins, vitamins and minerals. All five are food components that the body actively uses — for energy, for growth, for repair, for defence, for the hundreds of processes that go on without our noticing. Components that do this work are called nutrients.
The five major nutrients divide neatly by function: • Energy-giving nutrients — carbohydrates and fats • Body-building nutrients — proteins • Protective nutrients — vitamins and minerals
Vitamins and minerals earn the name protective nutrients because they defend the body against disease and keep it working properly. You need them in tiny quantities, and you need them without fail.

This is why you are told to drink milk, eat green vegetables, eat fruit, and eat whole grains rather than only polished ones — not because these foods are filling, but because they carry the nutrients that nothing else will supply.
Vitamin D is on the list, but one of its sources is not a food at all. Which one — and what does that tell you about spending time outdoors?
3.4 Cooking, Roughage and Water
Have you noticed that a raw carrot snaps and a boiled one bends? That spinach loses its bright green in the pan?

Heat changes food, and not only in ways we can see. Some nutrients — Vitamin C among them — are partly destroyed by high heat. Washing vegetables and fruit after cutting or peeling them washes some vitamins away as well.

Two sensible conclusions follow. First, include some fruit and raw vegetables in your diet so that not everything you eat has been through a hot pan. Second, wash produce before you cut it, not after.
But do wash it. Thoroughly, every time. The vitamins lost to washing are a small price against the dirt, pesticide residue and germs that washing removes.

items: Ira: So every nutrient we need comes from a plant or an animal?
Aarav: That's what the chapter says.
Ira: Then where does salt come from? Not a plant. Not an animal.
Aarav: Seawater. Or rock.
Ira: And Vitamin D — the teacher said our own skin makes it in sunlight. That isn't food either.

text: Ira is right on both counts, and there are two more things the body needs that are not nutrients at all.

Roughage, also called dietary fibre, comes mainly from plant foods — whole grains, pulses, fruit with its skin, green leafy vegetables, nuts. Roughage supplies no nutrients whatsoever. The body cannot digest it. That is precisely the point: it gives the digestive system bulk to work against, moving waste through and out. Without enough of it, the gut slows and constipation follows.

Water supplies no nutrients either, and nothing works without it. Water carries nutrients from the gut into the blood, carries waste out through sweat and urine, and holds the body's temperature steady. Drink it regularly through the day rather than in one gulp when you are already thirsty.
Which foods give you water besides water itself? List four.
Coluthur Gopalan (1918-2019)
If you want to advise an Indian family on what to eat, you need to know what Indian food actually contains. In the middle of the twentieth century, nobody did.

Coluthur Gopalan set out to find out. Over his career he and his colleagues analysed the nutritional content of more than five hundred Indian foods — not foods from foreign tables, but the grains, pulses, vegetables and greens that Indian households actually cooked. It is difficult, unglamorous laboratory work, and it produced something India had never had: reliable numbers for its own diet.

He then led large surveys of what Indians were eating and how healthy they were. The surveys found widespread shortages of protein and energy, particularly among children — not in a few unlucky families, but across whole populations.

Numbers of that kind are hard to ignore, and they changed policy. Gopalan's work fed directly into India's school meal programmes, including the Mid Day Meal Programme launched in 2002 and now run as PM POSHAN, which provides a cooked meal to children in government and government-aided schools. For millions of children it is the most nutritious meal of the day.
Gopalan died in 2019, aged 101.

Open Nutrient Detective on the classroom display. Build a day's meals from the food shelf and watch the nutrient bars fill as you add each item. Try to fill all five bars — then try again spending half as much money.
3.5 How Do We Test for Nutrients?

So far you have taken this chapter's word for it. Time to check for yourself. Some nutrients need a well-equipped laboratory to detect. Three do not: starch, fat and protein can each be tested with equipment a school already has. Starch, incidentally, is a carbohydrate — the form in which plants store it.

Before you begin, one habit worth building. Before each test, write down what you expect to happen. That written expectation is a prediction, and it is not a guess — it is your current understanding, put on record where the result can contradict it. A prediction that turns out wrong teaches you more than one that turns out right.

title: Activity 3.5 — Test for starch
items: You will need: small samples of potato, cucumber, bread or chapati, boiled rice, boiled gram, crushed peanut, oil, butter, crushed coconut; a dropper; dilute iodine solution; separate dishes.
1. Copy Table 3.3 into your notebook. Fill in the prediction column before you touch the iodine.
2. Place a small piece of each food on its own dish. Keep them apart and label them.
3. Note the colour of each sample before testing.
4. Using the dropper, put two or three drops of dilute iodine solution on each sample.
5. Watch for a colour change. Record what you see.
A blue-black colour indicates the presence of starch.
Which samples turned blue-black? Compare the result against your predictions. Where you were wrong, say why.

figure.caption: Fig. 3.7 — Testing food samples for starch

title: Activity 3.6 — Test for fat
items: You will need: the same food samples; plain paper.
1. Take a small piece of each food from Activity 3.5.
2. Place each on a separate piece of paper. Label the papers.
3. Fold the paper over the food and press firmly. Do not tear it.
4. If a food is watery, set the paper aside until it dries — a wet patch is not an oily patch, and confusing the two will ruin your result.
5. Hold each paper up to the light.
An oily patch that light passes through shows that the food contains fat.
Record your observations in Table 3.3.

Finish with three conclusions: starch present, fat present, protein present. Test potato, cucumber, boiled rice, boiled gram, peanut, bread or chapati, butter, coconut and one other food.

title: Activity 3.7 — Test for protein
items: Your teacher will demonstrate this activity. Read the precautions before anything else.
You will need: the same food samples; pestle and mortar; clean test tubes; two droppers; copper sulfate solution; caustic soda solution.
1. Grind each food sample into a paste or powder with the pestle and mortar.
2. Put about half a teaspoon of each into a separate clean test tube.
3. Add two or three teaspoons of water to each tube and shake well.
4. Using one dropper, add two drops of copper sulfate solution to each tube.
5. Using a different dropper, add ten drops of caustic soda solution to each tube.
6. Shake, then leave the tubes undisturbed for a few minutes.
A violet colour indicates the presence of protein.
Record your observations in Table 3.3.

precautions: Teacher demonstration — precautions. • Copper sulfate and caustic soda are harmful chemicals. Do not touch them unless your teacher tells you to. If any chemical touches your skin, wash the area with plenty of water at once and tell your teacher. • Never put these chemicals in your mouth. Do not try to smell them. Use a separate dropper for each chemical. Never return unused chemical to its bottle. Wash your hands when you have finished.

text: Read your completed table across the rows, not down the columns. Which foods showed more than one nutrient? Peanut should show both fat and protein. That is the finding that matters most here: a single food usually contains several nutrients at once. Foods are mixtures, not single substances — which is why a varied plate works better than a large one.
3.6 What Is a Balanced Diet?

Does everyone need the same food in the same amounts? Clearly not. A twelve-year-old is still growing and needs more protein for her size than her grandfather does. A farmhand doing heavy work all day needs more energy than someone at a desk. A person recovering from illness has different needs again. Requirements shift with age, sex, level of physical activity, state of health and way of life. A balanced diet is one that supplies all the nutrients a particular person needs, in the right amounts, together with enough roughage and water. Note the phrase a particular person. There is no single balanced diet for everybody — the idea only means anything once you say who is eating.

title: Activity 3.8 — Audit your own week
items: Go back to your food diary in Table 3.1.
1. Against each day, mark which of the five nutrients that day's food supplied.
2. Find the nutrient that is missing or thin most often.
3. Name two foods, available near you and affordable, that would fill the gap.
4. Do not redesign your whole diet. Change one thing, and keep it.

text: 3.7 Reading the Packet
Two snacks, both sold in a packet. Compare what is printed on them.

The wafers carry half again as much energy, five times the fat, roughly a third of the protein and under a third of the fibre. On the numbers, the chana is the better food by a wide margin — and it usually costs less. Foods high in sugar and fat but low in protein, vitamins, minerals and fibre are called junk foods: wafers, candy bars, carbonated drinks and much else sold as a snack. They deliver energy and little else. Eaten often, they crowd better food off the plate and lead to weight gain and the health problems that follow.
Find a real snack packet at home. Copy its nutrition panel into your notebook. Which column of Table 3.4 does it resemble?
3.8 Millets: The Grains That Came Back

Jowar, bajra, ragi, sanwa, kodo, kutki — these are millets, and they are among the oldest cultivated grains in India. For centuries they were ordinary food across large parts of the country. Then, within a few decades, they largely disappeared from urban plates, pushed aside by polished rice and refined wheat.

caption: Fig. 3.9 · Sanwa (barnyard millet) growing in a field

text: They are coming back, and the reason is nutrition.

Millets are small-grained cereals, so they supply carbohydrate like any cereal. What sets them apart is what comes with the carbohydrate: substantially more dietary fibre than polished rice, along with iron, calcium and B vitamins. Because of this they are often called nutri-cereals — cereals that carry protective nutrients alongside energy.

Millets are also easier on the land. They grow in poor soil, tolerate low and unreliable rainfall, and need far less water than rice. In a country where groundwater is falling in many districts, a grain that produces food on a fraction of the water is not a minor advantage.
So a millet does three useful things at once: it feeds a person better than polished rice, it grows where rice will not, and it uses less water doing it.
Would millets alone be enough?

No — and the reason is worth understanding. Millets are strong on carbohydrate, fibre and several minerals, but weak on some nutrients the body needs, and no cereal supplies everything. Eaten with dal, vegetables, milk or curd, millets make an excellent meal. Eaten alone, they leave gaps.
This is true of every single food, however good: the balance is in the plate, never in the item.
3.9 Food Miles: From the Field to the Plate

Aarav's lunch had rice in it. Ira's had wheat. Neither grew in the school. Follow a chapati backwards from the plate and you find a chain of work. A farmer prepares soil, sows wheat, waters and tends it for months, and harvests it. The grain is threshed and winnowed to separate it from the chaff. It is stored, often for months. It is transported to a mill and ground into flour. The flour is packed, transported again, and sold in a shop. Someone buys it, carries it home, kneads it, and cooks the chapati.
That is many months, many hands, and a great many kilometres, for one item on one plate.

title: Fig. 3.10 · The story of a chapati: from field to plate

text: The total distance a food item travels from producer to consumer is called its food miles. Shorter food miles are better on three counts. Transport costs money and burns fuel, so a shorter journey means cheaper food and less pollution. Food that travels less arrives fresher. And buying food grown nearby puts money into the hands of farmers near you rather than into transport along the way.
3.10 Food We Throw Away
Now put the two ideas together.
Everything on your plate carries months of a farmer's work and a long journey behind it. Food left uneaten on the plate throws all of that away — the water, the labour, the fuel, the months.
The remedy is not complicated and needs no equipment. Take what you will eat. Go back for more if you are still hungry. Finish what you have taken.
How would buying food grown near your town reduce its food miles? Trace the chain in Fig. 3.10 and mark which stages would get shorter.
Eat well. Share. Respect what is on your plate.
Buy from those who grow it.

Recap — the chapter in short

People across India eat widely different food, and the difference is not random. It follows the crops that grow in each region, which follow soil and climate, and is then shaped by culture, religion and taste.

Culinary practices have changed sharply within living memory — from chulha to gas stove, from sil-batta to mixer-grinder — driven by new technology, better transport and faster communication. The changes brought real gains and some real losses.
• Food is a mixture of components. The five major nutrients are carbohydrates, fats, proteins, vitamins and minerals. Food also supplies roughage and water, which are essential but are not nutrients.
• Carbohydrates and fats supply energy and are called energy-giving foods. Fat carries more energy per gram than carbohydrate and is the body's store.
• Proteins build and repair the body and are called body-building foods. Growing children and athletes need proportionally more.

• Vitamins and minerals are needed in tiny amounts and are called protective nutrients. Going short of one for long enough causes a specific deficiency disorder — scurvy, rickets, beriberi, goitre, anaemia — each with its own symptoms and its own food remedy.

• Roughage supplies no nutrients and cannot be digested; that is why it works, giving the digestive system bulk to move waste along. Water carries nutrients in, carries waste out, and holds body temperature steady.

• Starch, fat and protein can be detected with simple tests: iodine turns starch blue-black, fat leaves a translucent oily patch on paper, and copper sulfate with caustic soda turns protein violet. Most foods contain more than one nutrient.
A balanced diet supplies all the nutrients a particular person needs, in the right amounts, with enough roughage and water. What is balanced depends on age, sex, activity, health and way of life.

• Junk foods carry plenty of energy from sugar and fat and little else. Millets are called nutri-cereals because they carry fibre and minerals along with their carbohydrate, and they grow on less water.

• Food miles are the distance food travels from producer to consumer. Shorter is cheaper, fresher, less polluting, and better for nearby farmers. Wasted food wastes everything that went into producing it.
Practice — Recall
1. Pick the odd one out and give your reason. (i) Jowar, bajra, ragi, chana (ii) Kidney beans, green gram, soya bean, rice (iii) Papaya, carrot, mango, paneer

2. Name the nutrient and the food source you would recommend for each condition. (i) Bleeding gums and slowly healing wounds (ii) Difficulty seeing in dim light (iii) Soft, bent bones in a growing child (iv) Swelling at the front of the neck (v) Weakness and shortness of breath
3. Copy and complete:
In your notebook, compare the starch, fat and protein tests under these headings: What you add; Positive result; Nutrient detected.

4. State whether each is true or false, and correct the false ones. (i) Roughage supplies the body with energy. (ii) Fat carries more energy per gram than carbohydrate. (iii) Vitamin D can be obtained without eating anything. (iv) Table sugar is a protein. (v) A balanced diet is the same for everyone.

5. Give one word for each. (i) The distance food travels from producer to consumer (ii) Cereals rich in fibre and minerals, grown on little water (iii) The group of nutrients that protects the body from disease (iv) Dietary fibre, in one word (v) Common salt with iodine added
6. List the five major nutrients. Against each, write whether it is energy-giving, body-building or protective.
Use two notebook columns: Nutrient and Type (energy-giving, body-building or protective).
Practice — Apply

7. Ira eats biscuits, white bread and noodles, and avoids vegetables and fruit. She often has stomach ache and difficulty passing stool. Which component is missing from her diet? Name three foods she should add, and explain what each will do.

8. Reshma has trouble seeing in dim light. Her doctor prescribes a vitamin supplement and advises a change of diet. (i) Which deficiency disorder does she most likely have? (ii) Which nutrient is short in her diet? (iii) Name four foods she should include.

9. Gourav fractures his leg. His doctor sets the bone, applies a plaster, and prescribes calcium tablets. At the next visit the doctor adds Vitamin D syrup. Use Fig. 3.5 to answer: (i) Why calcium? (ii) Why add Vitamin D alongside it, rather than more calcium? (iii) What question would you want to ask the doctor?
10. You are offered canned fruit juice, freshly squeezed juice, and a whole fresh fruit. Which would you choose, and why? Give two reasons, at least one of them about a nutrient.
11. Sugar is a carbohydrate, but sugar tested with iodine does not turn blue-black. What does this tell you about the relationship between sugar and starch?

12. A drop of iodine solution falls on Ira's cotton socks and another on her teacher's silk saree. The drop on the saree turns blue-black; the drop on the socks does not. Suggest an explanation. (Think about what is used to stiffen cloth.)

13. A family lives in a district where the soil is low in iodine. They eat plenty of locally grown food and are not short of meals. Explain why a member of that family might still develop goitre, and what the simplest remedy would be.

14. Two snacks weigh the same. One lists 8 g protein and 3 g fibre per 100 g; the other lists 3 g protein and 1 g fibre, with twice the fat. Which is the better everyday snack? Justify your answer using the numbers.
Practice — Reason and Investigate

15. Raman says: "All starches are carbohydrates, but not all carbohydrates are starches." Is he right? Design an activity that would test his claim, stating what you would use, what you would do, and what result would support him.

16. You are handed an unlabelled solution and told it may be iodine solution. Describe how you would find out, using only what is in your kitchen. State what result would confirm it and what result would rule it out.

17. Millets grow on less water and carry more fibre and minerals than polished rice. Yet polished rice replaced millets across much of urban India. Suggest two reasons why a food that is worse on nutrition might still win. (Consider cost, cooking time, storage, and what people believe about food.)
18. Lind's 1746 comparison of two groups of sailors is described in Case 1. Why was it stronger evidence than one doctor's opinion about lemons? What would have made it stronger still?
Beyond the Book

• Read three labels. Next time groceries are unpacked at home, find three packaged items and copy their nutrition panels. Rank them from best to worst as an everyday food and write two lines defending your ranking.

Salt without a factory. The Apatani people of Arunachal Pradesh traditionally make a salt called tapyo from plant ash rather than from seawater or rock. Find out how, and why a community would develop such a method. Write a short account with pictures.

Wild food near you. In many parts of India people gather uncultivated greens, fruit and mushrooms — the ranbhajis of Maharashtra are one example. find out whether anything is gathered wild near your town. Ask an older person; they will know things the internet does not.

• Write to your principal. With your classmates, list the junk foods most often eaten in your school. Then write a joint letter to your principal proposing which to remove from the canteen and what to offer instead. Cost your alternatives — a proposal nobody can afford will be refused.
